title: Family Structure Is Key to Student Success: The Case for Federal Reporting in Education
gist: A new AEI/IFS report argues that family structure is as or more predictive of children's academic and mental-health outcomes than race, income, or sex — children in non-intact households are 13% less likely to earn A's and B's, 47% more likely to have parents contacted for school problems, and over twice as likely to be depressed — yet NAEP has collected family-structure data since 2013 without ever reporting scores by it on the Nation's Report Card.

themes.theme: The Missing Variable in Federal Reporting

insights.claim: The National Assessment of Educational Progress has been systematically collecting family-structure data since 2013 but has never reported student scores by family structure on the official Nation's Report Card.
insights.speaker: Ian Rowe, Brad Wilcox, and Grant Bailey
insights.so_what: A 13-year backlog of already-collected federal microdata that could be released without new surveys — a low-cost policy change with an immediate evidence shock.
insights.locator: The federal government collects a wealth of data

insights.claim: NAEP disaggregates student performance by race, ethnicity, sex, and poverty but not by family structure, creating a systematic asymmetry in which demographic explanations for achievement gaps get official federal amplification and family explanations do not.
insights.speaker: Ian Rowe, Brad Wilcox, and Grant Bailey
insights.so_what: Reporting choices shape which causal narratives dominate education policy and funding flows; changing them redirects the debate and the money.
insights.locator: The National Assessment of Educational Progress from the US Department of Education disaggregates

insights.claim: The authors' policy ask is that family structure become a standard and consistent data category across Department of Education reports and every federal agency monitoring child well-being, including in analyses of child-wellbeing surveys.
insights.speaker: Ian Rowe, Brad Wilcox, and Grant Bailey
insights.so_what: A concrete, cheap regulatory ask with an aligned AEI/IFS coalition behind it — watch for adoption as a signal of the family-policy agenda gaining institutional traction.
insights.locator: To remedy this, key federal reports

themes.theme: Family Structure Outpredicts Race and Income

insights.claim: In a new AEI/IFS analysis of the National Survey of Children's Health, family structure is as or more predictive of key child outcomes than race, family income, and student sex.
insights.speaker: Ian Rowe, Brad Wilcox, and Grant Bailey
insights.so_what: If family structure dominates race and income as a predictor, the standard demographic controls in education and health research are underspecified — a direct challenge to the prevailing analytic frame.
insights.quote: In a new AEI/IFS analysis of the National Survey of Children’s Health, family structure is as or more predictive of key outcomes than race, family income, and student sex.

insights.claim: Children in non-intact households — stepfamilies, cohabiting parents, single parents, foster or kin-based homes such as grandparent-led households — are 13% less likely to receive A's and B's than children raised by married biological or adoptive parents.
insights.speaker: Ian Rowe, Brad Wilcox, and Grant Bailey
insights.so_what: Puts a specific effect size on the achievement penalty from family structure, a magnitude comparable to interventions that receive far more education funding.

insights.claim: Children in non-intact households are 47% more likely to have their parents contacted for problems at school, making behavioral referrals the largest measured family-structure gap in the analysis.
insights.speaker: Ian Rowe, Brad Wilcox, and Grant Bailey
insights.so_what: School behavioral-incident load — a major driver of teacher attrition and district costs — tracks family structure more tightly than test scores do.
insights.locator: more likely to have their parents contacted

insights.claim: Children in non-intact households are more than twice as likely to be depressed than children in intact married-parent homes.
insights.speaker: Ian Rowe, Brad Wilcox, and Grant Bailey
insights.so_what: A 2x depression differential links family structure directly to the adolescent mental-health crisis and to pediatric behavioral-health demand.
insights.locator: more than twice as likely to be depressed

insights.claim: Family structure is reported as a more powerful predictor of school problems, academic performance, and depression than either race or poverty in this analysis.
insights.speaker: Ian Rowe, Brad Wilcox, and Grant Bailey
insights.so_what: Explicitly ranks family structure above the two variables that dominate education policy discourse — the report's core against-consensus claim.
insights.quote: family structure is a more powerful predictor of school problems, academic performance, and depression than are race and poverty

insights.claim: The authors explicitly hedge that their findings are not necessarily general results and call for further study to determine how far the predictive strength of family structure generalizes.
insights.speaker: Ian Rowe, Brad Wilcox, and Grant Bailey
insights.so_what: The caveat matters: this is a single-survey correlational result being deployed for a federal reporting mandate, so expect methodological pushback.

themes.theme: Second-Order Effects of Publishing the Data

insights.claim: Publishing outcomes by family structure would displace what the authors call incomplete or misleading narratives about the causes of educational, health, and economic disparities.
insights.speaker: Ian Rowe, Brad Wilcox, and Grant Bailey
insights.so_what: The strategic aim is narrative reframing of disparity debates — a shift with implications for how remediation dollars are allocated across schools and social services.
insights.quote: move beyond incomplete or misleading narratives about the causes of educational, health, and economic disparities
insights.locator: These data insights would empower key stakeholders

insights.claim: A stated goal of federal family-structure reporting is behavioral feedback: showing young people how family types map to child outcomes so they become more proactive about their own future family formation.
insights.speaker: Ian Rowe, Brad Wilcox, and Grant Bailey
insights.so_what: This is an information-based fertility and marriage intervention — cheap, scalable, and an early template for how pro-family policy may be pursued without subsidies.
insights.quote: thus making them more proactive regarding their own future family formation
